table.text: Our approach to power analysis for the single-slope model was a Monte Carlo simulation, similar to the method suggested for mixed-effect models by Hox et al. (2018). We defined a fixed-effects linear model to determine the correlation between each teacher emotion and each dimension of instructional quality, using one teacher emotion each as the predictor, one dimension of instructional quality as the criterion, and the countries as dummy-coded clustering variables. We then simulated 10,000 samples to determine how many simulated data sets would result in the teacher emotion in question being a significant predictor after the standard errors had 2 √1 + (𝑚 -1) × ICC; m = average cluster size, ICC = intra-cluster correlation 3 ICC predictor × ICC model_residual been corrected using the square root of the unconditional design effect. This allowed us to determine the critical effect size for reaching a power of at least .90, given the sample size of N = 652 teachers in the Global Teaching InSights Study.
table.header: 4.5.1 Strategic Approach to Power Analysis for Detecting a Single Slope

table.text: Using the above specifications (N = 652, ICC = .10, power = .90), the resulting critical effect size for a linear model with cluster-specific intercepts for eight clusters was determined at 𝛽 = .25 (Figure 1 shows statistical power as a function of the magnitude of the standardized slope). Of the effect size estimates we gained based on existing literature, the association between teacher anxiety and social-emotional support is lower than this critical effect size at 𝛽 = -.19. We therefore excluded the corresponding hypothesis H3.2 from the registered confirmatory analyses. We merely examined this link in clearly marked exploratory analyses. We considered this power analy-sis sufficient grounds for analyzing all other associations.
table.header: 4.5.3 Power Analysis Results for Detecting a Single Slope

table.text: Effects for teacher anxiety are comparable to those for teacher anger, with a median of 𝛽 = -.30. Classroom management shows moderate-to-large or large effects with a median of 𝛽 = -.54. For socialemotional support, the picture is more mixed, with Hagenauer and Hascher (2018) reporting only a small and Burić and Frenzel (2023) a small-to-moderate effect, resulting in a median effect of 𝛽 = -.19. Instruction yields mostly moderate effects, though small effects are reported by Czerniak (1989) for number of methods and Trigwell (2012) for conceptual change focus; Burić and Frenzel (2023) also found a smallto-moderate effect of teacher anxiety for cognitive engagement. Note. Power estimates for each point on the curve calculated using 1,000 simulated samples.
table.header: 4.5.2 Literature Review to Determine Expectable Effect Sizes for Emotion-Instructional Quality Links

table.text: Having no empirical basis for assuming specific degrees of variability in the slopes for each country, we again used a simulation approach to ascertain how strongly the country-level slopes would need to differ for a likelihood-ratio-test to identify the model with an interaction term as superior. For our simulation, we assumed that slopes would be equally distributed. Our simulation yielded that a range-or difference between the smallest and largest slope-of standardized 𝛽s for the prediction of a certain dimension of instructional quality by the teachers' enjoyment, anger, or anxiety rating of 𝛽 = .50 could be detected at a power of .90 (see Figure 2 for the power curve, with power as a function of the range of the standardized slopes). In other words: Assuming the eight country-level slopes were roughly equally distributed, the smallest slope was 𝛽 = .10, and the largest slope was 𝛽 = .60, this would result in a significant likelihood-ratio-test. In such a case, we would use the model with an interaction term for that spe-cific combination of a teacher emotion and a dimension of instructional quality. Note. Power estimates for each point on the curve calculated using 1,000 simulated samples.

info.title: Teacher Emotions and Instructional Quality: Insights from the Global Teaching InSights Video Study (Registered Report)

text.text: Existing research into the link between teachers' emotions and the quality of their lessons has generally relied either on students' or teachers' ratings of instructional quality and drawn on teacher samples from homogeneous cultural contexts.

The present study addressed these limitations by employing data from the multi-national Global Teaching InSights Study, in which 652 mathematics teachers in eight countries in East Asia, Europe, and South America self-reported their experiences of enjoyment, anger, and anxiety about teaching, and expert raters assessed instructional quality along the three established dimensions of classroom management, social-emotional support, and instructional support.
We used fixed-effects linear models to obtain estimates for the covariation between self-reported trait emotions and observer-rated instructional quality dimensions.

For social-emotional support and teacher anger / teacher anxiety, links were negative and significant; for social-emotional support and teacher enjoyment, links were positive but did not reach statistical significance.
These effects were largely homogeneous across the international samples, as exploratory analyses revealed.
For classroom management and instructional support, effects were negligible in size, and specifically teacher enjoyment-instructional support links were highly internationally heterogeneous.

These findings provide essential insights into how teachers' internal emotional experiences translate into their outward instructional behaviors, and the nuances brought about by varying assessment approaches for instructional quality.
The observed cross-country variability may spark future cross-national, cross-cultural research in this domain.
Great lessons inspire, poor lessons bore and annoy-and some teachers deliver great lessons far more often than others.

The crucial role of instructional quality for students' learning is wellestablished (Hattie, 2003 (Hattie, , 2023;; Ruiz-Alfonso et al., 2020), as is the fact that it varies substantially (Mullis et al., 2020).

text.text: A deeper understanding of the sources of differences in instructional quality across teachers may prove decisive in the quest to improve the quality of instruction worldwide.
Prior research shows that instructional quality is closely linked with a wide array of cognitive, moti-vational, emotional, attitudinal, and contextual factors.

For example, one area which past research (Baumert et al., 2010; Fauth et al., 2019; Kunter et al., 2013) has consistently emphasized concerns teachers' different types of knowledge, i.e., content knowledge, pedagogical knowledge, and pedagogical content knowledge (Shulman, 1987).

text.text: The present study seeks to add to this literature.

The specific research question addressed by our study is whether teacher self-reported experiences of enjoyment, anger, and anxiety are systematically correlated with observerrated instructional quality, across a broad and diverse range of eight countries on three continents: Chile, the People's Republic of China, Colombia, Germany, Japan, Mexico, Spain, and the United Kingdom.
This is also intended to help answer the question whether pleasant teacher emotions broadly correlate with higher instructional quality and unpleasant ones with lower instructional quality.
For this, we utilize data from the Global Teaching InSights Study (Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development [OECD], 2020c).

The Global Teaching InSights Study represents the first major international study to systematically collect data on secondary school mathematics teachers' self-reported classroom emotions as well as video-based observer ratings of instructional quality (Opfer, 2020a).

text.text: The body of research on teacher emotions has also clearly shown that teachers vary in their tendencies to experience different emotions: Some habitually experience stronger and more frequent teaching enjoyment, some tend to react with anger more often and more intensely than others during teaching, yet others experience anxiety during teaching more frequently and intensely (Frenzel et al., 2016).

text.text: Existing literature on discrete teacher emotions has commonly focused on teacher enjoyment, teacher anger, and teacher anxiety.

text.text: Assessing the links between teacher emotions and instructional quality is far from straightforward; one reason for this is that instructional quality is a hotly debated, highly complex phenomenon.
Classroom teaching takes place in a multi-faceted social environment, and researchers disagree on the exact scope of the term "instructional quality" (Charalambous & Praetorius, 2023).

text.text: In the present contribution-in line with the Global Teaching InSights Study-we adopt a view that has gained theoretical consensus across different strands of instructional quality research and has received extensive empirical support: It rests on the idea that instructional quality resides in deep structures of teaching, which can be conceptualized in separate dimensions.

One of the well-established strands of instructional quality research coined in the German research community posits that instructional quality can best be described through the three dimensions classroom management, student support, and cognitive activation (Klieme et al., 2001; Praetorius et al., 2018).

text.text: In the Global Teaching InSights Study, it is simply referred to as "instruction," and the present paper will follow that terminology.

It is further separated into four subdimensions: "Discourse" covers aspects like the quality of explanations given by the teacher, facilitating learning through appropriate questions, or whether students speak sufficiently often compared to the teacher.

"Student cognitive engagement" concerns the question whether students are actively engaged in trying to solve a problem using multiple different approaches while understanding the necessary processes and procedures.

"Assessment of and responses to student understanding" relates to whether teachers manage to entice students to convey their thoughts and whether teachers are then able to dynamically adapt their teaching to students' present understanding.

text.text: Instructional quality is notoriously difficult to measure.

Researchers often use student or teacher ratings; however, students have difficulty determining if a lesson is cognitively engaging in a way that is conducive to learning, and they often cannot differentiate between overwhelmingly difficult lessons and cognitively engaging ones (Fauth et al., 2020; Kunter & Baumert, 2007; Sigurjónsson et al., 2022).

text.text: An alternative approach is to have a trained third party observe a lesson and rate its quality.

Advantages of external ratings, compared to teacher or student reports, include not only the absence of self-representation bias or sympathy halo effects (Feistauer & Richter, 2017; Röhl & Rollett, 2021), but also optimized conceptual validity and measurement specificity through the use of structured rating manuals (see, e.g., Bell, 2020) and the professional knowledge of external raters regarding instructional quality (Kunter & Baumert, 2007), especially compared to laypeople as raters, whose assumptions about what good teaching entails can skew results (see Flink et al., 1990).

text.text: Affective science suggests that emotions, cognition, motivation, and behavior are closely intertwined.

Accordingly, in her model on causes and effects of teacher emotions, Frenzel (2014) posits that the emo-tions teachers experience influence their cognition, motivation, and behavior and thus shape the quality of their teaching through a range of psychological mechanisms, while teachers' behaviors influence student behaviors and outcomes, which in turn influence their emotions (see also Burić & Frenzel, 2023; Frenzel et al., 2021).

text.text: While data used in the present study do not allow for an analysis of causal directions, the theoretical foundations for current research into teacher emotion-instructional quality links, with the reciprocal model at their center, make certain assumptions about directions of influence.
Grounding our research in relevant theory thus requires the inclusion of causal assumptions that will not be empirically tested by the present study.
One mechanism through which teacher emotions likely affect their teaching behavior is that of cognitive processing styles.

According to the "Broadenand-Build Theory," pleasant emotions positively impact individuals' cognitive flexibility and creativity (Fredrickson & Branigan, 2005; Sugawara & Sugie, 2021), which are both of great importance in the complex and unpredictable classroom environment.

text.text: It is therefore also a reasonable proposition that repeated experiences of pleasant emotions during teaching fuel teachers' willingness to invest time and effort in lesson preparation, while frequent and intense expe-riences of anger or anxiety ought to coincide with avoidance of teaching-related activities outside of school, hence reducing lesson preparation quality and time.

Above and beyond those proposed effects from emotions on instructional quality, Frenzel and colleagues also emphasize the systemic nature of classroom processes which involves close and reciprocal interconnections between all actors' behaviors (Frenzel et al., 2009 (Frenzel et al., , 2021)).

text.text: Hence, efficient and successful teaching, bringing about few disturbances and high student engagement, can be expected to positively impact teachers' confidence and self-efficacy levels and in turn promote positive emotions like enjoyment, whereas delivering instruction of poor quality undermines teachers' confidence and sense of control over teaching activities and can therefore give rise to experiences of negative emotions such as anger and anxiety (for initial empirical evidence on such reciprocal effects between instructional quality and teacher emotions in Germany and Croatia, see Burić & Frenzel, 2023).

text.text: Overall, there are compelling theoretical reasons for assuming that high quality instruction will coincide with heightened levels of teacher enjoyment, while poor quality instruction will be linked with elevated levels of teacher anger and anxiety.
However, the existing evidence for such links between teacher emotions and instructional quality is still scarce.

With the present study, we set out to add to this evidence by exploring those links using observer ratings of instructional quality across several countries world-wide, using the Global Teaching InSights data (OECD, 2020c).

Given that, the additional question arises whether and to what degree emotions can be expected to be functionally equivalent across cultures and countries and whether and to what degree the emotions teachers experience in class can thus be assumed to covary with their teaching behavior in similar ways across cultures and countries.

The question of culture-specificity versus universality of emotions is contentious within broader affective science (Barrett, 2016; Barrett et al., 2025; De Leersnyder et al., 2021; Ekman, 2018; Keltner et al., 2019; Mesquita et al., 2016).

text.text: Following this reasoning, we propose that the degree to which teachers from different cultures and contexts report enjoyment, anger, and anxiety during teaching may well differ across cultures and contexts, and the frequency and qualitatively manifested manner of showing certain teaching-quality-related behaviors may well vary across the various countries sampled in the Global Teaching InSights Study.
However, the general direction of links between teacher emotions and their instructional behavior should be similar across those countries.
Specifically, we propose that across countries, teachers' enjoyment should be positively linked with several facets of teaching quality, while teacher anger and anxiety should show negative links.
At the same time, we do not exclude the possibility that the strengths of these generally positive and negative links may vary across different cultural contexts.

For example, it is conceivable that (classroom) cultures characterized by higher power distance across teachers and their students may be marked by stronger links between teacher anger and classroom management, as teachers in such cultures more strongly externalize their anger in terms of disciplining behaviors (which in turn may not even be perceived as particularly controlling by the students in these cultures, e.g. Zhou et al., 2012).

text.text: In turn, it is also conceivable that teacher-reported anger shows weaker links with observer-rated teaching behaviors in cultures where display rules make the outward expression of anger culturally inappropriate; teachers may internally experience anger but not show corresponding outward behavior which observers could perceive and rate according to its impact on instructional quality.
For the specific context of the present study, it is important to note that "culture" is not equivalent to "country."

text.text: Hence, we proposed that the Global Teaching InSights Study's international, unprecedentedly large teacher sample is highly suitable to test for the general direction of teacher emotion-teaching quality links and therefore the overall functional role and theoretical plausibility of teacher emotions as decisive factors for classroom dynamics.
However, it did not seem particularly suitable to substantiate any main or moderating effects of culture.

For these reasons, we focused our directed hypotheses on general expected patterns across the full Global Teaching InSights sample, while planning to addition-ally explore potential differences between countries in an open-ended manner.

In exploring potential links between teachers' selfreported emotions and observer-rated instructional quality, this study addresses important gaps in existing research: A lack of outside observer perspectives and a lack of cross-national analyses.
First, past studies have commonly assessed instructional quality via teachers' or students' reports.
As explained previously, this approach does not capture all aspects of instructional quality equally well.

It is worth noting that it is by no means trivial to assume that subjective, internal emotional experiences as reported by teachers indeed manifest themselves in terms of behaviors implying higher or lower levels of instructional quality as observable to external one-time "visitors" of a classroom.
Yet the theory provided above on cognitive, behavioral and motivational implications of emotional experiences provides compelling grounds for assuming this.

Second, previous studies concerning the link between teacher emotions and instructional quality have usually been limited to a single country or conducted on a per-country basis, whereas both instructional quality and teacher emotions are highly relevant phenomena in classrooms all over the world.

This study takes advantage of data from eight different countries on three continents, covering a range of both industrialized and emerging countries from the Global Teaching InSights Study (OECD, 2020c), which represents the first major international study to collect data on secondary school mathematics teachers' self-reported classroom emotions as well as observer ratings of instructional quality based on classroom videos (Opfer, 2020b).

text.text: Based on our previous considerations on relative universality of teacher emotions and cross-national / cross-cultural comparability of broader dimensions of instructional quality, we suspected that we would find similar effects for each country in the sample, but we allowed for the possibility of significant differences.
Exploring in detail the degree to which the relationships between teacher emotions and facets of instructional quality potentially vary is therefore an additional benefit of this study.

In view of the relatively large overall teacher sample size of the Global Teaching InSights Study, the present study has substantial potential for advancing our under-standing of teacher emotions, instructional quality, and their interrelations.

text.text: The overarching research question for the present study is whether and to which extent teacher emotions in mathematics classrooms worldwide are linked to observable facets of instructional quality.
We hypothesized that teachers' self-reported enjoyment would be positively associated with observers' ratings of classroom management (H1.

Conversely, we expected that teachers' self-reported anger (H2.1, H2.2, H2.3, H2.3.1, H2.3.2, H2.3.3, and H2.3.4, respectively) and anxiety (H3.1, H3.2, H3.3, H3.3.1, H3.3.2, H3.3.3, and H3.3.4, respectively) would be negatively associated with those facets of instructional quality.
We additionally explored whether the strength of each of these correlations varies significantly between countries.
Due to the limited theoretical basis, we refrained from stating hypotheses of either equivalence or specificity.

text.text: Previous literature linking teacher emotions with instructional quality has not so far employed observer ratings of instructional quality, but has usually relied on student ratings, making these studies quite different from the proposed analysis of the present study.

While existing research does not provide sufficient information to conclude whether observer ratings of instructional quality should correlate with teacher emotions as much as student ratings do, a useful parallel is research linking teacher self-efficacy with instructional quality: In their meta-analysis, Klassen and Tze (2014) found comparable overall effect sizes for student ratings of instructional quality, at a median of r = .20 for student ratings and r = .21 for observer ratings.

text.text: Thus, for a construct that is fairly closely related to teacher emotions conceptually and that relies on teacher self-reports in its measurement, effect sizes for student reports and observer ratings are comparable, bolstering the estimates for our power analysis.

In conclusion, we consider the parameters extracted from existing literature on teacher emotion-instructional quality links informative for estimating plausible effect sizes for our novel exploration of the correlation between teacher emotions and observer-rated instructional quality-despite the fact that previous studies have relied on instructional quality ratings by teachers or students.

Having no empirical basis for assuming specific degrees of variability in the slopes for each country, we again used a simulation approach to ascertain how strongly the country-level slopes would need to differ for a likelihood-ratio-test to identify the model with an interaction term as superior.

text.text: 5 Results

Self-reported teacher enjoyment across the countries was on average fairly high and both teacher anger and teacher anxiety were relatively low, judged by the means on the four-point Likert scale ranging from 1 to 4.
Descriptive statistics for the instructional quality variables have already been reported in the Global Teaching InSights Study's main report (OECD, 2020c).

Out of the dimensions of instructional quality, classroom management scored very high across all countries (see also Bell, Castellano, & Klieme, 2020); social-emotional support was moderate (see also Bell, Klieme, & Castellano, 2020) and instruction overall relatively low, with somewhat higher ratings for the sub-dimensions discourse and assessment of and responses to student understanding and somewhat lower ratings for student cognitive engagement and quality of subject matter (see also Bell, Schweig, et al., 2020).

text.text: In addition to the descriptive statistics laid out in the registered analysis pipeline, we also report per-country intra-cluster correlations in the last column of Table 2, as they are crucial for interpreting the subsequent regression model results.

What becomes apparent is that much of the total variability for these dimensions was determined by country so that intra-cluster correlations for the various variables in the study were generally high-typically higher than the value of .10 which we had used in the power analysis (see above), especially for the instructional quality dimensions.
This implies relatively large adjusted standard errors and thus potentially lower-than-expected statistical power for the main analyses.

text.text: Pearson correlations between the three selfreported teacher emotions were substantial; teacher enjoyment negatively correlated with teacher anger and teacher anxiety, while teacher anger and teacher anxiety correlated positively with each other.
The sub-dimensions of instructional quality also showed moderate to strong correlations with each other.

Intriguingly, the correlations (not accounting for country-level differences in instructional quality ratings, which were considered in the main regression models reported below) showed partly counter-expected directions between the teacher emotions and the instructional quality ratings: Teacher enjoyment was uncorrelated with social-emotional support, weakly negatively correlated with classroom management, and negatively correlated with instruction.
Teacher anger and anxiety, in turn, were uncorrelated with classroom management and instruction, but-more in line with expectations-showed negative correlations with social-emotional support.

As detailed in our registered analysis pipeline, for each pair of a teacher emotion and a dimension or sub-dimension of instructional quality, we fitted two models: One with a single slope across all countries and one with an interaction model featuring countryspecific slopes.
The more complex interaction model did not, for any pair of variables, significantly outperform the model using a single slope; likelihoodratio-tests yielded between p = .10 and p = .99.
We therefore proceeded with the single-slope approach for every regression model.

text.text: Counter to Hypotheses H1.1, H1.3, and H1.3.1-3, teachers' self-reported enjoyment was not significantly linked with observer ratings of classroom management and the higherorder instruction composite, nor the sub-dimensions of instruction.

However, in line with H1.2, there was a positive trend for the relationship between teacher self-reported enjoyment and observer ratings of social-emotional support, although this effect did not reach the threshold for statistical significance.

Findings were similar for teachers' selfreported anger: We found no effects for instruction or its sub-dimensions (H2.3 and H2.3.1-3) and only a non-significant negative trend for the correlation between teacher self-reported anger and observer-rated classroom management (H2.1).
Further, there was a significant negative correlation between teacher self-reported anger and observerrated social-emotional support.

Lastly, none of the registered hypotheses regarding teacher anxiety (H3.1, H3.3, and H3.3.1-3) yielded any significant effects; however, the exploratory result for teacher anxiety predicting social-emotional support (H3.2), which had been excluded from the registered hypotheses, was significant.

text.text: Per-country links between teacher emotions and dimensions of instructional quality revealed noticeable heterogeneity between countries.
Teacher enjoyment and classroom management showed positive links for three of the eight countries, as well as an unexpected substantial negative link for Colom-bia.
The other countries showed no clear links, and none of the effects were statistically significant.

For teacher enjoyment and social-emotional support, there were substantial positive effects for six out of eight countries, four of which were significant, whereas the other two effects were negligible.
For instruction, there were once again three clear positive effects, one negative effect, and four negligible effects.
None of the teacher enjoyment-instruction links exceeded 𝛽 = ±.10 by much, and only one (China) was significant.

Sub-dimensions of instruction showed positive or insubstantial links with teacher enjoyment except for a negative effect of teacher enjoyment on student cognitive engagement in Germany and a negative effect of teacher enjoyment on assessment of and responses to student understanding in Japan.

Regarding teacher anger and classroom management, there were three negative effects in line with expectations; this effect was significant only in the United Kingdom, while in the remaining five countries, this effect was too small to interpret.
The per-country effects of teacher anger and socialemotional support were clearer, with five substantial negative effects, three of which were significant, and only three negligible ones.
For teacher anger and instruction, there were only two substantial links, one of which (Germany) was, contrary to our hypotheses, positive.
None of these effects were significant.

Subdimensions of instruction showed overall weak links with teacher anger, except for the unexpectedly positive associations of teacher anger with discourse and student cognitive engagement in Germany.

When further scrutinizing these observed variabilities of the emotion-instructional quality links, one noticeable pattern we identified was the comparatively larger apparent effects in European countries compared to South American and East Asian nations.

In our study, we aimed to analyze whether teachers' self-reported enjoyment, anger, and anxiety during teaching and observer-rated aspects of instructional quality are linked in accordance with the reciprocal model on causes and effects of teacher emotions (Frenzel, 2014; Frenzel et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In our study, we aimed to analyze whether teachers' self-reported enjoyment, anger, and anxiety during teaching and observer-rated aspects of instructional quality are linked in accordance with the reciprocal model on causes and effects of teacher emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Frenzel, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Frenzel et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: We utilized data from the international Global Teaching InSights Study and derived effects across all countries.

The highly plausible theoretical underpinnings rooted in general affective science and Frenzel's reciprocal model as well as results from prior studies employing teacher or student ratings of instructional quality both suggested a high likelihood of finding moderately strong effects.

However, we have-among our confirmatory analyses-only found one single statistically significant predictive effect that holds across all countries in the sample: A negative association between teacher-reported anger and observer-rated social-emotional support.
Teacher-reported anxiety, too-while being excluded from our confirmatory analyses-showed a negative significant link with observer-rated social-emotional support.

Teacherreported enjoyment showed a trend towards positive correlation with observer-rated social-emotional support with a similar absolute effect size as the negative effects for anger and anxiety, but this effect did not reach statistical significance. 4Overall, the present study showed that the more anger and, at least from an exploratory perspective, the more anxiety teachers reported feeling when teaching the target class, the less the external observers found those teachers to demonstrate emotionally and socially supportive behaviors.

text.text: Notably, these effects only became fully evident when controlling for country-level differences in teaching quality ratings in the multiple-regression approach and were partially masked in the overall correlative findings.
This highlights the importance of considering country-level differences in a large cross-national sample, such as the Global Teaching InSights Study.

We also observed a statistically non-significant effect indicating that teachers' enjoyment may correlate with higher levels of observed social-emotional support, which in our opinion warrants further scientific inquiry in future research.

What teachers reported to feel on the inside indeed seems to reflect in their outward relational behavior, but not in their didactical or classroommanagerial behavior, as judged by external observers.

This finding that social-emotional support stands out as the one dimension of instructional quality that is most clearly linked with teachers' emotions makes sense conceptually: The overall emotional tone of the classroom as well as the level of negativity (including anger) present are both aspects of this dimension (Hamre et al., 2013).

text.text: Raters in the Global Teaching InSights Study used the quantity and severity of negative interactions in the classroom as well as shared warmth between teachers and students as indicators for social-emotional support (OECD, 2020b), both of which are reasonably linked with teachers' inward experiences of enjoyment and anger.
The Global Teaching InSights Study's third indicator for social-emotional support focused on students' risk-taking and their propensity to freely share their work or ask questions.

Links with such classroom events and teachers' emotional experiences makes sense in view of existing research, such as Frenzel et al. (2016), who found that teachers' enjoyment correlates positively and teacher anxiety negatively with their acceptance of students' errors, which ought to influence students' preparedness to risk being wrong or asking a "stupid" question.

(2016)</ref>, who found that teachers' enjoyment correlates positively and teacher anxiety negatively with their acceptance of students' errors, which ought to influence students' preparedness to risk being wrong or asking a "stupid" question.

text.text: Importantly, though, except for these consistent but small teacher emotion-social-emotional support behavior links, our findings otherwise amounted to null-findings regarding the teacher emotion-instructional quality links.
This contrasts with previous research (see Appendix, Table A3) generally finding moderate effects of teacher emotions across several instructional quality dimensions and contexts.

text.text: Below, we provide three possible explanations for this.

The uniqueness of the present study lay in its assessment approaches: This is the first study which linked teacher emotions assessed via self-report with instructional quality assessed via expert ratings of instructional quality based on classroom video recordings.
Teachers' emotional self-reports reflect their internal experiences of emotions during teaching, which may well diverge from how these emotions-and their consequences-become visible on the outside.

Classroom display rules, variability in teacher emotional expressiveness, and emotion regulation effectiveness may explain those discrepancies (Frenzel et al., 2025; Matsumoto, 1990; Safdar et al., 2009; Taxer & Gross, 2018; Wang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Classroom display rules, variability in teacher emotional expressiveness, and emotion regulation effectiveness may explain those discrepancies <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Frenzel et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Matsumoto, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">Safdar et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b171">Taxer & Gross, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b179">Wang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As such, the present null-findings for effects of teacher emotions on their externally judged instructional quality (except for social-emotional support) may be explained by the potential fact that teachers on average are sufficiently successful at regulating their emotions, hiding or suppressing their negative experiences in class, to deliver decent levels of instructional quality irrespective of how they feel on the inside (see also Wang & Frenzel, 2025, regarding the double-edged function of surface acting among teachers).

text.text: Consequently, there is a possibility that previous studies not employing observer scores may have overestimated the effect of teacher emotions on instructional quality.

Prior research which used teachers as the data source for both their own emotions and instructional quality may well have suffered from some effect overestimation due to singlesource bias (Podsakoff et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Prior research which used teachers as the data source for both their own emotions and instructional quality may well have suffered from some effect overestimation due to singlesource bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">(Podsakoff et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Further, even studies that used students as observers-hence circumventing single-source bias-may have delivered over-estimated effects as students may be subject to psychological distortions such as halo effects (Röhl & Rollett, 2021): They may thus rate enthusiastic and joyful teachers more highly across a number of dimensions (also referred to as "educational seduction" or "Doctor Fox effect", see Naftulin et al., 1973, which, however, has been more or less refuted in more recent literature: see Frenzel et al., 2019; Peer and Babad, 2014).

text.text: Finally, there is also a possibility that existing research is affected by publication bias and thus studies which-like this study-had previously found statistically insignificant results may exist but have never been published.

Besides their respective potential for distortions, teachers, students, and external observers also perceive essentially different aspects of instructional quality (Fauth et al., 2020; Kunter & Baumert, 2007).

text.text: Thus, there is another reasonable explanation for our unexpected null findings: It is possible that aspects of instructional quality of which teachers are more aware or which students notice more acutely are more tightly linked to teacher emotions.
This link may, conversely, be much weaker for aspects of instructional quality which outside observers notice.
This hinges on the idea that each of these data sources have their own unique perspective on instructional quality with its own specific validity (Fauth et al., 2020; Kunter & Baumert, 2007).

text.text: It is also possible that teacher emotions interact more closely with aspects of instructional quality that become visible over a longer time frame (see Praetorius et al., 2014).
text.formatted: It is also possible that teacher emotions interact more closely with aspects of instructional quality that become visible over a longer time frame (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b139">Praetorius et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The two lessons covered by the Global Teaching InSights Study may have been too short a time frame to capture certain facets of instructional quality (according to our findings, likely from the domains of classroom management and instruction) that are more visible in teacher or student ratings.
Finally, it is very plausible that distortions in the Global Teaching InSights Study's measurements masked existing effects.

For one, the raters for the Global Teaching InSights Study were not present during the lessons but judged instructional quality based on classroom videos, and the impression of a lesson derived from a recording is substantially different-and potentially less accurate-than what a live observer would perceive (Curby et al., 2016).

text.text: This may have, for example, distorted raters' ratings of classroom management by altering their impression of how noisy the classroom was at a given moment, or relevant events may have happened out of frame.
It must also be acknowledged that the Global Teaching InSights data have clear psychometric limitations.

Interrater reliability between raters as well as agreement between raters and master raters were not especially high across the domains (Castellano & Bell, 2021), and while our analysis of across-country reliabilities showed sufficient internal consistency, the same cannot be said for all scores within individual countries for both instructional quality ratings (Castellano & Bell, 2021) and teacher emotion self-reports (Mihaly et al., 2021).

text.text: Regarding the Teacher Emotions Scales, in Spanish-speaking countries, the internal consistencies were also quite low, specifically for teacher anger, which was lowest in Mexico at 𝛼 = .58, and teacher anxiety, which was lowest in Colombia at 𝛼 = .49 and also unsatisfactory in Spain at 𝛼 = .59.

Developing internationally applicable, objective, reliable, and valid observation instruments and processes is notoriously difficult (Bell et al., 2015), as is the creation of multi-language questionnaires that are applicable across different linguistic contexts and cultures (Dong & Dumas, 2020; J. text.text: Our study may therefore well be underestimating the true effects.

Hence, future improvements to instructional quality measurements in high-fidelity observational studies like the Global Teaching InSights Study may eventually reveal stronger effects than the ones obtained in the present study.

Sample characteristics between the countries were also notably different (see Appendix, Table A4): For example, average student age was 13.78 years in Spain compared to 16.58 years in Chile, which, in addition to cultural differences, likely limited betweencountry comparability.

text.text: This variability in sample characteristics may be a contributing factor for the large intra-cluster correlations (see Supplement, table S6), which increased standard errors and thus p-values in this study considerably.

text.text: Additionally, sampling bias is present in the Global Teaching In-Sights Study's dataset, with only Colombia achieving a fully representative national sample of secondary school mathematics teachers and Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom all relying on convenience sampling.
A second key distinction of the present study compared to its predecessors was its diverse international teacher sample.

Our exploratory investigation of per-country effects revealed, first, that the as-sumption of relative universality (Pekrun & Goetz, 2023) largely held up: We did not observe the variance across countries to be statistically significant.
text.formatted: Our exploratory investigation of per-country effects revealed, first, that the as-sumption of relative universality <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">(Pekrun & Goetz, 2023)</ref> largely held up: We did not observe the variance across countries to be statistically significant.

text.text: The direction of effects was largely equivalent across countries and in line with theory, though it must be stressed that this purely exploratory observation should not be mistaken for a significant, confirmatory result.
Nevertheless, we also observed a large degree of heterogeneity and a couple of notable exceptions with counter-expected directions of effects.

Those exceptions included Colombia, where teacher enjoyment negatively predicted classroom management; Japan, where teacher enjoyment negatively predicted assessment of and responses to student understanding; Spain, where anxiety positively predicted the same sub-dimension; and Germany, where teacher enjoyment negatively predicted instruction and especially the student cognitive engagement sub-dimension, while anger positively predicted instruction and its sub-dimensions.
Since the focus of this paper was not on per-country effects and these values were derived from exploratory analyses, we refrain from speculating about these particular exceptions in detail.

Further, our last exploratory analyses highlighted an intriguing tendency: There was a significantly stronger positive link between teacher enjoyment and classroom management and a significantly stronger negative link between teacher anger and classroom management in more individualistic (Hofstede, 2001; Minkov & Kaasa, 2022) countries.

text.text: Both methodological and substantive factors may have contributed to this finding.

For instance, the scales originally developed in one culture may not demonstrate the same psychometric characteristics when 'imported' into another culture (F. F. Chen, 2008), potentially also compromising opportunities to detect cross-scale covariation in the 'importing' culture.

text.text: On a more substantial note, a possible explaining factor could be stricter emotion display rules within more collectivistic cultures (Safdar et al., 2009), which may have mitigated some potential positive effects of expressing enjoyment as well as potential negative effects of expressing anger on observed classroom management.

text.text: While this should only be considered a preliminary exploratory result for the purposes of this registered report, it certainly provides an intriguing angle for future research.
There are also clearly a myriad of differences between the eight countries in this specific sample that may likewise explain the heterogeneity of the effects.

These range from systemic differences between their educational systems (see Table A4) to economic factors to cultural factors that are more specific and multi-faceted than the unidimensional collectivism-individualism axis.

text.text: Therefore, future research into the role of cultural differences regarding the teacher emotions-instructional quality link may benefit from assessing teachers of different cultural backgrounds who work inside comparable institutional frameworks, e.g., by choosing teachers from a culturally diverse country such as the United States (see Leung & Cohen, 2011).
text.formatted: Therefore, future research into the role of cultural differences regarding the teacher emotions-instructional quality link may benefit from assessing teachers of different cultural backgrounds who work inside comparable institutional frameworks, e.g., by choosing teachers from a culturally diverse country such as the United States (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Leung & Cohen, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Future research into the links between teacher emotions and instructional quality across national contexts may benefit from focusing on the socialemotional support dimension in particular, as it showed the closest links in our analyses.

Clearly, there is a need for larger sample sizes; specifically to explore, on a more fine-grained level, the ways teacher emotions interact with classroom contexts and cultural contexts in their effects on instructional behavior.
This is a challenging, but potentially fruitful endeavor that may, for instance, benefit from mixed-methods approaches in combination with large-scale international educational assessment projects.
Instructional quality remains an intriguing and highly relevant field of research, but its assessment is subject to numerous theoretical and methodological idiosyncrasies.
Teacher emotions share these attributes.
This complexity is again increased by taking the international and intercultural view.

In our study, we took a step towards investigating the interrelations between self-reported teacher emotions and expert ratings of instructional quality, using a large international sample of teachers.
We found a significant negative effect for the link between teachers' negative emotions (anger and anxiety) and social-emotional support.
We also found a nonsignificant trend for a positive effect of teacher enjoyment.
For the dimensions of classroom management and instruction, there were no significant effects and negligible effect sizes.

This large percentage of insignificant and null effects puts this study into stark contrast with previous findings that had relied on more homogeneous samples and teacher or student ratings of instructional quality.
Our findings and deliberations may serve as springboards for future cross-national, cross-cultural research into teacher emotions, instructional quality, and their interrelatedness.
